tagline: A mining road from Fairbanks to Circle on the Yukon
intro: The Steese Highway runs from Fairbanks to Circle on the Yukon River, with much of the road narrow and winding. Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights the Chatanika River, access to the White Mountains National Recreation Area and the midnight sun at Eagle Summit at summer solstice. The full highway extends 161 miles from Fairbanks to Circle, ending about 50 miles south of the Arctic Circle.

The road was built to serve the Circle Mining District, productive in the 1890s before gold discoveries in the Klondike. Completed in 1927, it took the name of General James G. Steese, a former Alaska Road Commission president. Mining remains part of its roadside story: the preserved camp at Chatanika and active dredging operations line the route. The Chatanika camp was built in 1925 by the Fairbanks Exploration Company, which also dug the Davidson Ditch to supply water to its dredges.

Leaving Fairbanks, the highway follows Alaska Route 2 to Fox, then Route 6 for most of the remaining journey. Gold Dredge Number 8 stands on the old Steese between Fairbanks and Fox. Beyond Chatanika, Central’s museum interprets mining and displays mammal remains from Mammoth Creek. Circle ends the drive beside the Yukon, where river freight once supplied the gold camps.

moments.title: Gold Dredge Number 8
moments.text: Five decks and a length of 250 feet give Gold Dredge Number 8 the scale of an industrial operation. The Fairbanks Exploration Company operated this ladder dredge from 1928 to 1959 on the old Steese Highway between Fairbanks and Fox. Beginning in the 1920s, the 90-mile Davidson Ditch brought water into the area for mining. The dredge cut a 4.5-mile track. Its later recognition included National Register listing as a historic district in 1984 and designation as a Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark in 1986. Alaska’s transportation department includes tours of the dredge among its byway highlights.

moments.title: Central
moments.text: Central’s Circle District Historical Society museum pairs mining history with remains of pre-glacial Alaskan mammals found in Mammoth Creek. Alaska’s transportation department identifies Central with one of the state’s most active mining districts. The Steese Highway passes through town.

moments.title: Circle
moments.text: Circle began as a transfer point between river freight and inland gold camps. Established in 1893 after gold was discovered in Birch Creek, it received supplies shipped up the Yukon from the Bering Sea. By 1896 it was the Yukon’s largest mining town, with 700 residents. Gold discoveries in the Klondike in 1897 and Nome in 1899 drew away much of that population. The name outlasted a geographical mistake: miners thought they had reached the Arctic Circle, which lies about 50 miles farther north. Mining continues in the area into the twenty-first century.
